newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-TIGER TACKLES TROON FOR FIRST TIME.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER TACKLES TROON FOR FIRST TIME.

text.p: Tiger Woods tackled Royal Troon for the first time on Monday and strengthened his playing partners' conviction he has all it will take to win the British Open on Sunday.

Golf's new shooting star, already the U.S. Masters champion and world number one at the age of 21, played a casual round with his good friend and neighbour in Florida, Mark O'Meara, and fellow Americans John Cook and Dudley Hart.
Woods, who will give a news conference on Tuesday, declined several invitations to comment after his round.
"I'll talk to you all tomorrow," he said repeatedly.
But O'Meara, who has become Woods's mentor on Tour, was impressed about his friend's approach to his first look at the 7,079-yard course on the west coast of Scotland.
"I think he handled it just fine," O'Meara said. "He likes to play little knockdown shots, creative shots like you have to do here.
"If he plays like he can do, there is no reason why he can't win. His confidence is high and he is very talented beyond his 21 years.
"If he keeps his composure and plays smart golf, there is no reason why he can't do well."
O'Meara said he and Woods were friends despite their age difference of 19 years.
"I like his company," he said. "The challenge for me is to find a way to beat him."
Cook, second to Nick Faldo in the 1992 Open at Muirfield, was also upbeat in his assessment of Woods.
"The thing about Tiger is that he doesn't think he's got the world beat," Cook said. "He's learning, he's not afraid to ask questions, he observes a lot.
"He is very much in control of his golf. He doesn't hit a driver off every tee. He has impressed just about everybody.
"I think he has handled things pretty well. It is not easy," Cook added.
Woods's coach, Butch Harmon, said he felt his protege "was a little amazed how difficult it is to pick your targets because of the flatness and lack of definition on the fairways.
"You have to aim at landmarks, corners of grandstands, that sort of thing.
"But I think he can win anywhere," Harmon added.
Woods and company set off down the first fairway under the watchful eyes of some 400 spectators and four marshals calling themselves "crowd-beaters".
The marshals were present to prevent the crowd from getting too close, but there were no problems.
"We're basically crowd-beaters but we hope we won't have to beat up any crowds," one of them said before Woods began.

Michael Bonallack of the Royal and Ancient Club, which stages the Open, said the marshals' job "was to make sure the people don't badger him too much so he can concentrate on golf and not have to sign autographs all the time".
Bonallack added that a police officer might be assigned to Woods later in the week.
Woods, who has won seven titles since turning pro last summer, made it clear from the outset he was not out to humble the course on his first visit.
With a slight wind behind, he might have tried his luck at driving the greens on the relatively easy opening holes, but he spurned the opportunity.
His drive at the 364-yard first finished in rough some 40 yards short of the green.
At the 391-yard second and the 379-yard third, he used irons off the tee for safety -- a significant clue to his plan of attack on Thursday.
He found more rough off the tee at the 557-yard fourth and his escape shot landed short of the green and took a sharp bounce left.
Woods is playing in his third British Open. He was still amateur when he finished joint 66th at St Andrews and joint 22nd at Royal Lytham last year.
His round complete and reporters rebuffed, Woods disappeared into the stately old Royal Troon clubhouse.
He emerged a few minutes later and charged off towards his nearby hotel, the four marshals surrounding him as he walked.
